title: The Performance Engineering Mindset
blurb: Tests why a single timing misleads, how to benchmark with warm-up, repetition and robust statistics, Amdahl's Law and its hard ceiling, why measured speedup falls short past the physical core count, and how to use Amdahl as a sanity check before optimising.

questions.prompt: Why did one naive timing of a small NumPy matmul read 15.3 ms when the median was 1.18 ms?
options: The first call paid for one-time library setup, like the BLAS threads.
The matrix was larger on the first call, before it was cached.
perf_counter is inaccurate below 20 ms, so it rounds up.
The first call used a different, slower algorithm for the multiply.
questions.explanation: One-time initialisation lands in the first measurement and has nothing to do with steady-state speed. It is the same trap as the first CUDA launch paying for context setup.

questions.prompt: The single measurement was 15.261 ms and the median 1.178 ms. By what factor did it overstate the cost? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 15.261 / 1.178 = 12.95, about 13.0x. The single number was close to the slowest of all 200 runs.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter warn against reporting the mean alone?
options: The mean is always lower than the true cost, so it flatters the code under test.
The mean ignores the warm-up runs, which are the most important.
The mean can't be computed from timeit's output.
A few OS interruptions can drag it upward. Minimum and median are more robust.
questions.explanation: Scheduling noise adds outliers on the slow side. The minimum shows best-case steady state, and the median shows typical cost with moderate noise.

questions.prompt: In Procedure 48.1, what is each statistic for?
options: Minimum for typical cost, mean for the worst case
Median for the best case, maximum for typical cost
Mean for the best case, minimum for the worst case
Minimum for best case, median for typical cost
questions.explanation: The procedure reports min for "what's the best this can do" and median for "what does this typically cost". The mean is included but shouldn't stand alone.

questions.prompt: When is a quick single perf_counter timing acceptable?
options: For any number reported to a manager, since it is simple to explain
When comparing two implementations that differ by more than 10%
As a rough gut check, never for comparing options
Whenever the operation takes longer than one second
questions.explanation: A gut check is fine. Comparisons and reported numbers need warm-up and repetition, since noise alone can flip a single-shot comparison.

questions.prompt: According to Amdahl's Law, what caps speedup as workers go to infinity?
options: The number of physical cores on the machine
The serial fraction s, giving a ceiling of 1/s
Nothing. Speedup grows without limit.
The memory bandwidth, giving a ceiling of bandwidth × cores
questions.explanation: Speedup(N) = 1 / (s + p/N) tends to 1/s. Cores and bandwidth are real-world limits, but not what the formula expresses.

questions.prompt: A program is 95% parallelisable. What is its maximum possible speedup with unlimited workers?
questions.explanation: s = 0.05, so the ceiling is 1 / 0.05 = 20x, however many cores you add.

questions.prompt: At 32 workers, measured speedup was 4.81x against Amdahl's 7.25x. Why the gap?
options: Python can't start more than 16 processes at once.
The measurement was wrong, since Amdahl's Law is exact.
Overheads Amdahl ignores, plus hyperthreads past 16 cores.
The serial fraction grew to 50% at 32 workers.
questions.explanation: Process spawning, communication and contention aren't in the formula, and hyperthreads share a core's execution resources. The gap is a lesson, not an error.

refLinks.label: §48.2.2 Amdahl’s Law: The Ceiling You Can Compute in Advance

options: Using multiprocessing instead of threads for CPU-bound work
Extrapolating linearly past the physical cores
Testing with more workers than physical cores at all
Measuring the one-worker baseline before the others
questions.explanation: The curve bends past 16 on the reference rig. Linear extrapolation into hyperthreads overestimates real throughput for CPU-bound work.

questions.prompt: What does Amdahl's Law assume that Gustafson's law changes?
options: A fixed problem size, while Gustafson scales the problem with the hardware
A fixed number of cores, while Gustafson allows the core count to grow
Zero serial work, while Gustafson allows some
Perfect caching, while Gustafson models cache misses
questions.explanation: Amdahl asks how much faster a fixed job gets. Gustafson's regime grows the job as hardware grows. The chapter names it without covering it in depth.

questions.prompt: A team wants 20x from parallelism, and profiling shows a 30% serial fraction. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Add more cores until 20x is reached, since Amdahl's Law is only a forecast.
The ceiling is about 3.3x, so shrink the serial part or change the plan.
Parallelise harder, since the serial fraction shrinks as workers grow.
Use hyperthreads, which bypass the serial fraction.
questions.explanation: 1 / 0.3 = 3.3x. The chapter's point is the sanity check: if the ceiling is below the goal, more workers is the wrong plan.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 48.2 warn against estimating the serial fraction by intuition?
options: Intuition always overestimates it, which makes plans too cautious.
The serial fraction changes every run, so it can't be estimated at all.
Amdahl's Law only accepts serial fractions measured by perf.
It often measures 15–20% when it feels like 5%, from I/O or locks.
questions.explanation: Profile it (Chapter 50). Underestimating s overstates the ceiling, which is how teams end up chasing impossible speedups.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter separate its own topic from "avoid premature optimisation"?
options: This chapter says to optimise first and measure later.
Measuring correctly against acting in the right order.
Avoiding premature optimisation means never using Amdahl's Law.
They are the same rule under two names.
questions.explanation: Measuring correctly and profiling before acting are related but distinct. Both matter, and Chapter 50 covers the profiling side.

questions.prompt: How did the worked example estimate the serial fraction s?
options: By fitting Amdahl's curve to all six measured speedups
The known 0.3 s setup over the one-worker wall-clock time
From perf counters that separate serial and parallel instructions
By guessing 10% and checking it against the 32-worker run
questions.explanation: p = 1 − 0.3 / times[1], so s = 0.3 / times[1] ≈ 0.110. Knowing the serial cost directly made the estimate simple.

questions.prompt: At 2 and 4 workers, measured speedup was slightly above Amdahl's prediction. How does the chapter read that?
options: As a sign that the serial fraction was negative
As scheduling noise, with the tracking still close
As proof that Amdahl's Law underestimates real speedup
As an error in the one-worker baseline
questions.explanation: Small gaps of −0.08 and −0.26 are noise. The meaningful gap opens past the physical core count.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why the single naive measurement of `compute()` (15.261 ms) was so much larger than the 200-repetition median (1.178 ms). Name the specific mechanism responsible.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The single naive measurement included one-time NumPy/BLAS first-call initialisation costs (loading libraries, JIT-warming internal routines) that a repeated benchmark's warm-up phase absorbs and discards. The 200-repetition median reflects steady-state cost only, after that one-time overhead has already been paid once and excluded.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague reports "I sped up my function by 3x" based on one `time.perf_counter()` call before and one after. Using this chapter's single-measurement trap, write two or three sentences on why this claim shouldn't be trusted yet.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A single before/after measurement cannot distinguish a real 3x improvement from ordinary run-to-run noise (system jitter, scheduling, cache state, background load). This chapter's own single-measurement trap shows a single reading can be off by ~12x from steady state. The claim needs a repeated, warmed-up benchmark reporting median or minimum before it's trustworthy.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 48.1, benchmark two implementations of a function that sums the squares of a list of 100,000 integers: a plain Python loop and a list comprehension. Report the median time for each and state which is faster on your machine.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Answer depends on the machine, but the loop version is expected to be several times slower than the list comprehension for a 100,000-element sum-of-squares, since the comprehension avoids repeated Python-level `append` calls and bytecode dispatch overhead per iteration. Report whichever medians are actually measured on the machine running the exercise.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 48.2, compute Amdahl's ceiling and the realistic 8-worker speedup for a pipeline profiled at 22% serial. State whether reaching a 6x speedup goal for this pipeline is achievable with any amount of added parallelism.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With $s = 0.22$: Amdahl's ceiling is $1/s = 1/0.22 \approx 4.55$x. The realistic 8-worker speedup is $1/(0.22 + 0.78/8) = 1/(0.22+0.0975) = 1/0.3175 \approx 3.15$x. A 6x speedup goal is not achievable at any worker count, since it exceeds the $4.55$x ceiling that holds even with infinite workers.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter's Amdahl table shows measured speedup slightly *exceeding* the prediction at 2, 4, and 8 workers, before falling short at 16 and 32. Propose an explanation for how measured speedup could exceed an idealized theoretical prediction at all, given that Amdahl's Law assumes zero overhead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Amdahl's Law assumes the parallel work divides perfectly evenly with zero overhead. Real hardware can exceed the naive prediction if, for example, more workers collectively use more aggregate cache or reduce single-core memory contention in ways the simple serial/parallel split doesn't model. Small positive effects like better cache utilisation per worker can transiently outweigh coordination overhead until the physical core count is exceeded and contention starts to dominate instead.

bookExercises.prompt: A team wants to parallelize a workload currently taking 10 hours, and needs it under 1 hour. Profiling finds the serial fraction is 8%. Using Amdahl's ceiling, write the two or three sentences you would tell this team about whether their goal is achievable by adding workers alone.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With $s = 0.08$: ceiling $= 1/0.08 = 12.5$x. Going from 10 hours to under 1 hour requires more than 10x speedup, which is below the 12.5x ceiling. So the goal is theoretically achievable, but only with enough workers to approach that ceiling closely, and real overhead (per this chapter's own measured gap past the physical core count) means the team should expect to need meaningfully more than the naive Amdahl worker count to actually hit 10x in practice.

bookExercises.prompt: Read Amdahl's original 1967 paper (or a reliable secondary summary). Identify one assumption in the original argument that this chapter's empirical measurement (the growing gap past 16 workers) directly demonstrates breaking down in practice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Amdahl's original argument assumes a fixed problem size with zero coordination/communication cost between workers. This chapter's growing gap past 16 workers (the physical core count) directly demonstrates that assumption breaking down. Hyperthread contention and real scheduling overhead are exactly the "zero overhead" assumption failing in measurable practice.

bookExercises.prompt: Read enough of Gustafson's "Reevaluating Amdahl's Law" to state, in your own words, how the "scaled speedup" framing differs from Amdahl's fixed-problem-size framing. Give one example of a real workload where Gustafson's framing is the more honest way to talk about parallel scaling.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only. Gustafson's scaled-speedup framing holds the *work per worker* fixed and lets total problem size grow with the number of workers, rather than holding total problem size fixed as Amdahl does. Appropriate for workloads like scientific simulations at increasing resolution, where more hardware is used to do a *bigger* job in the same time, not the same job faster.
